summary: Describes extensions for Transport Layer Security, including generic mechanisms for adding data to the TLS client and server hellos plus specific extensions built on them. They are backward compatible with clients and servers that lack them. It obsoleted RFC 3546 and updated RFC 4346, and was replaced by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers can add optional extras to their first hello message and still work fine with ones that do not know about the extras.

subtitle: A way for TLS clients and servers to add optional features to their opening hello messages without breaking older software.

tldr.problem: TLS was now used in environments its designers had not envisioned, such as wireless networks with limited bandwidth, memory and power, and it had no standard way to add optional features.
tldr.mechanism: An extended client hello and extended server hello carry a list of typed extensions. Six specific extensions are defined on top of this: server name, maximum fragment length, client certificate URLs, trusted CA keys, truncated HMAC and certificate status request.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4366 obsoleted RFC 3546 and updated RFC 4346, and it was in turn obsoleted by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066.

today: RFC 4366 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 3546 and updated RFC 4346. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5246 and RFC 6066 and updated by RFC 5746, so those are the documents to read for current rules.

sections.title: Why TLS Needed Extensions
sections.content:
TLS was by this point used in a growing range of environments, many not foreseen in its original design. Wireless environments often have bandwidth, computational power, memory and battery limits. The extensions are meant to let TLS work as effectively as possible there.

The document gives both generic extension mechanisms for the client and server hello messages and specific extensions built on them. New cipher suites are explicitly left out. A key design goal is backward compatibility: clients with extensions can talk to servers without them, and the other way round. This works because TLS already requires servers to ignore added data in the client hello that they do not recognize. Some constrained clients may still have to refuse servers that lack an extension.

This document is a revision of RFC 3546. The one major change is that new extensions can now be defined via the IETF Consensus Process rather than needing a standards track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Some gadgets are tiny and slow, like a toy walkie-talkie. These extras let them tell the other side what they can handle, while bigger computers just ignore what they do not understand.

sections.title: The Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
A client MAY send an extended client hello, which is the normal ClientHello followed by a client_hello_extension_list. A server answers with an extended server hello carrying a server_hello_extension_list, and only in response to an extended client hello, so existing clients are never surprised.

Each extension is an Extension structure holding an extension_type and opaque extension_data. The types defined here are server_name(0), max_fragment_length(1), client_certificate_url(2), trusted_ca_keys(3), truncated_hmac(4) and status_request(5). IANA maintains the list.

An extension type MUST NOT appear in the server hello unless it appeared in the client hello, and a client MUST abort the handshake if it sees one it did not ask for. There MUST NOT be more than one extension of the same type. A server that supports the mechanism MUST check that a client hello matches exactly the original or extended format, otherwise it sends a fatal decode_error alert.

Two new handshake messages are added, certificate_url(21) and certificate_status(22). If a session is resumed, the server MUST ignore the extensions and send a server hello with none of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The first hello is like a note with an optional extras box at the bottom. The other side can only fill in the extras box if you asked for those extras first.

sections.title: The Six Specific Extensions
sections.content:
Server name indication (server_name) lets a client tell the server which host name it wants, which helps when one network address hosts many virtual servers. The name is a UTF-8 DNS host name without a trailing dot, and literal IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are not permitted. A server that uses it answers with an empty server_name extension.

Maximum fragment length (max_fragment_length) lets constrained clients ask for fragments of 2^9, 2^10, 2^11 or 2^12 bytes instead of the default 2^14 bytes.

Client certificate URLs (client_certificate_url) let a client send a CertificateURL message in place of a full certificate, saving memory. Servers that support it MUST support the http: scheme. If a SHA-1 hash is given, the server MUST check it and otherwise abort with a bad_certificate_hash_value alert.

Trusted CA indication (trusted_ca_keys) lets a client with few root keys say which it holds, to avoid repeated handshake failures.

Truncated HMAC (truncated_hmac) cuts the MAC to 80 bits, so only the first 10 bytes of the HMAC output are sent and checked.

Certificate status request (status_request) asks the server to send an OCSP response in a CertificateStatus message right after its Certificate message, saving the client from fetching a revocation list.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six extras. You can say which website you want, ask for smaller pieces, send a web link to your ID card instead of the card itself, say which authorities you trust, use shorter checksums, and ask for proof that the server's ID is still valid.

sections.title: New Error Alerts and Defining New Extensions
sections.content:
Five new alerts are defined: unsupported_extension(110), certificate_unobtainable(111), unrecognized_name(112), bad_certificate_status_response(113) and bad_certificate_hash_value(114). They MUST NOT be sent unless the other party has sent an extended hello.

New extension types are assigned by IANA through the IETF Consensus process, which in practice means RFCs approved by the IESG. The RFC advises that extensions should be designed so an attacker cannot force use or non-use of a feature by tampering with handshake messages, and that using extensions to change major aspects of TLS, such as cipher suite negotiation, is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong with an extra, there are new warning messages to say exactly what. And new extras can only be added after grown-ups on a committee agree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Each extension gets its own analysis. The most serious concern is client_certificate_url: the server acts as a client of another URL protocol, so an attacker might use it to attack another host or to drive denial of service. The RFC RECOMMENDS that this extension be specifically enabled by an administrator, not on by default, and that only a minimal set of URL protocols be enabled.

Omitting the certificate hash saves effort but exposes the client to an attack using a different valid certificate on the same key. For truncated_hmac, truncated MACs may be weaker, but no significant weakness was known for HMAC with MD5 or SHA-1 truncated to 80 bits. For status_request, a client that requires OCSP validation SHOULD contact the OCSP server itself or abort if the server does not support the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The risky extra is the one where the server fetches a web link for you, because a trickster could point it at someone else's door. So it should be switched on only on purpose.
